query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled isothermal aging treatment at 750 °C for 2 hours of a Ti–Ni–based HEA (composition Ti30Ni30Al10Cr10Co10 in at%) will precipitate uniformly distributed, nanoscale coherent sigma phase particles within the alloy’s BCC/B2 matrix, leading to a significant improvement in elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance (expected >20% improvement) compared to an as-solutionized alloy without aging.
generation.material_initial_state: A solutionized single-phase HEA obtained by heating to ~1150 °C to ensure a homogeneous BCC/B2 matrix in a Ti–Ni–based alloy with the nominal composition Ti30Ni30Al10Cr10Co10 (with Ti and Ni as the primary constituents).
generation.intervention: Subjecting the solutionized alloy to an isothermal aging treatment at 750 °C for 2 hours in an inert atmosphere, with precise control of temperature and time to induce the precipitation of sigma phases.
generation.conditions: The alloy operates under elevated temperature conditions up to approximately 700 °C. The intervention is applied after solution treatment on a Ti–Ni primary HEA with fixed compositional boundaries (Ti30Ni30Al10Cr10Co10 in atomic percent) and in an inert (non-oxidizing) atmosphere.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a uniform, nanoscale dispersion of coherent sigma (intermetallic) precipitates distributed within the BCC/B2 matrix.
generation.mechanism: Precipitation strengthening via the coherent sigma precipitates, which impede dislocation motion and transfer load efficiently. The fine precipitate network acts to enhance yield strength and retard creep deformation at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under mechanical testing at around 700 °C, the aged alloy is expected to exhibit a significant increase in yield strength and improved creep resistance (anticipated improvement >20%) relative to the same HEA processed only with solution treatment.
generation.baseline: A Ti–Ni primary HEA with the same composition (Ti30Ni30Al10Cr10Co10) that is only solutionized at ~1150 °C and not subjected to the aging treatment, thereby retaining a single-phase microstructure without the beneficial sigma precipitates.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable for the specified HEA composition (Ti30Ni30Al10Cr10Co10) and under operating temperatures up to approximately 700 °C. The controlled aging parameters (750 °C for 2 hours) are critical and form the boundaries within which the predicted improvements are anticipated.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in yield strength and creep resistance as well as the long-term stability of the sigma precipitates at temperatures slightly above 700 °C remain to be fully determined. Variabilities in precipitate size distribution and volume fraction could affect outcomes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples with the same HEA composition (Ti30Ni30Al10Cr10Co10), one set subjected to the controlled solution treatment at ~1150 °C only (baseline), and the other set to the same solution treatment followed by aging at 750 °C for 2 hours. Conduct identical elevated-temperature mechanical tests on both groups.
measurements: Yield strength at ~700 °C using high-temperature compression/tensile tests
Creep rate measurements under constant load at 700 °C
Microstructural analysis via TEM or SEM to quantify precipitate size, distribution, and volume fraction
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged samples do not show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., >20% increase in yield strength and notable creep resistance enhancement) compared to the unaged samples, or if the predicted uniform precipitation of sigma phases is not observed, the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This study uses molecular dynamics to investigate the effects of grain size gradient structure, cutting depth, cutting-edge radius, and rake angle on CoCrNi MEAs during conventional cutting. The conclusions are: (1) The cutting chips transform into a mixed-phase structure of FCC and HCP. The plastic deformation at small average grain sizes is mainly dominated by grain boundary slip and grain rotation. The grains release energy as the machining proceeds and merge into larger grains. Grain boundaries do not affect partial dislocations when the grain size is large enough. (2) The average resultant force decreases with increased average grain size, which indicates a Hall–Petch relationship. Moreover, the cutting force increases with increased cutting depth, cutting-edge radius, and negative rake angle. (3) The stress is concentrated in the front of and below the cutting edge and transmitted through the grain boundaries. The improvement of properties of directionally solidified (DS) eutectics with microstructure refinement has been related to a Hall–Petch relationship for eutectics. For Al–Si eutectics, there are different hardness versus inter-lamellar spacing relationships for different silicon morphologies []. Mason et al. showed that the hardness of a Mo5Si3/MoSi2 eutectic depended on lamellar spacing in accordance with a Hall–Petch relationship, where the hardness was dependent upon the scale of the lamellae of MoSi2 []. Dislocation pile-ups are necessary for Hall–Petch strengthening. Grain boundaries impede dislocation propagation from one grain to the next. As the dislocations pile up against a grain boundary, the stress field assists dislocations to traverse the grain boundary, and thus, deformation spreads from grain to grain. Dislocations are generated during indentation for the measurement of hardness []. For the Mo5Si3/MoSi2 eutectic, Mason et al. suggested that the Mo5Si3 silicide behaved as an impenetrable barrier [].

The in-situ composites containing of FeCrNiCu high entropy alloy matrix and SiC particles were designed and prepared by vacuum electromagnetic induction melting. The reaction process of the Si-Ni-C system consists of one step; i.e., Si reacting with C to form SiC particles as reinforcement phase. The activation energy of the reaction was found to be 1302.8 kJ/mol. The matrix of the as-sintered composites is mainly composed of Cu-rich phase and Cu-poor phase. The mechanical properties of the composites are significantly improved by the presence of SiC reinforcement phase. The hardness of SC10 is 78.3% higher than that of the matrix. The tensile strength of the composite is 846.0 MPa, which is 49.6% greater than that of the matrix. The multiple strengthening mechanisms were identified; namely, dislocation strengthening, load bearing effect, Orowan mechanism and solid solution strengthening. Among them the major contribution is from dislocation strengthening, which raised the tensile strength of the matrix by 58.6%.

The heat treatment at 1100 °C for 1 h on the Al0.8NbTiVM0.2 (M = Co, Ni) alloys results in the formation of the sigma particles within the BCC matrix. The formation and homogeneous distribution of sigma particles plays a critical role in enhancement of yield strength in heat-treated Al0.8NbTiVM0.2 (M = Co, Ni) alloys. Moreover, the high-temperature compression tests (700 and 800 °C) were conducted for the Al0.8NbTiVM0.2 (M = Co, Ni), and the comparison of the temperature dependence of yield strength was made via the specific yield strength (yield strength/density). The specific yield strength of the Al0.8NbTiVM0.2 (M = Co, Ni) alloys is superior to single-phase AlNbTiV and NbTiVZr RHEA alloys and conventional Ni-based superalloy (Inconel 718 alloy) at elevated temperatures up to 700 °C.

proposals.material_system: Ti–Ni–based HEA with minor additions (e.g., Ti30Ni30Al10Cr10Co10 in at%)
proposals.intervention: Introduce a controlled heat‐treatment aging step to precipitate coherent intermetallic (sigma) phases by a minor addition of Al
proposals.conditions: Solutionized at ~1150 °C, then aged isothermally at 750 °C for 2 hours in an inert atmosphere
proposals.structural_mediator: Nanoscale coherent sigma/intermetallic precipitates homogeneously dispersed within the BCC/B2-type matrix
proposals.mechanism: Precipitation strengthening: The coherent precipitates hinder dislocation motion at elevated temperatures, thereby increasing yield strength and creep resistance relative to the as-cast alloy
proposals.predicted_outcome: Elevated-temperature mechanical tests (e.g., at 700 °C) will show a significant increase (>20%) in yield strength and improved creep resistance compared to the same HEA without aging
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By forming a stable reinforcing phase in a Ti–Ni primary HEA, this intervention directly exploits precipitation strengthening—a well‐established mechanism—to enhance high-temperature mechanical properties that have not been previously explored with Ti and Ni as primary constituents

proposals.intervention: Apply a severe plastic deformation process (high-pressure torsion, HPT) followed by a short, low-temperature anneal
proposals.conditions: HPT processing at room temperature with an imposed shear strain >100 followed by annealing at ~600 °C for 30 minutes in vacuum
proposals.structural_mediator: Ultrafine-grained (submicron) microstructure with high-angle grain boundaries
proposals.mechanism: Grain boundary strengthening via the Hall–Petch effect, where the refined microstructure resists dislocation motion and enhances high-temperature mechanical performance
proposals.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventionally processed HEA, the HPT-treated alloy will exhibit at least a 15–25% improvement in yield strength and better creep resistance at elevated temperatures (around 650–700 °C)
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: Refining the microstructure in a titanium–nickel primary alloy leverages mechanical processing—a different mechanism from compositional tweaking—to improve high-temperature strength, offering a process-based route to enhanced properties

proposals.material_system: Ti–Ni–primary HEA (for example, Ti35Ni35Mo10Cr10Al10 in at%)
proposals.intervention: Deposit a thin high-temperature-stable hafnium-based surface coating via high-vacuum radiofrequency sputtering
proposals.conditions: Sputter deposition using an HVRF system at low ion densities (e.g., ~20 µA/cm²) to form a ~400 nm coating, with no post-deposition heat treatment, followed by high-temperature oxidation testing (e.g., 1600 °C for 5 h in air)
proposals.structural_mediator: A well-adhered, diffusion-bonded Hf-rich oxide/diffusion barrier layer that forms an integrated transition layer with the substrate
proposals.mechanism: Enhanced oxidation resistance: The coating impedes oxygen ingress and minimizes oxidation-induced microstructural degradation, thereby indirectly preserving the mechanical integrity of the Ti–Ni alloy during high-temperature exposure
proposals.predicted_outcome: The coated alloy will exhibit a significantly lower oxidation weight gain (e.g., <50% of that measured for the uncoated alloy) along with superior retention of yield strength after high-temperature exposure
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By addressing the degradation mechanism (oxidation) that can weaken elevated-temperature performance, this coating strategy offers an external, protective intervention that complements the intrinsic mechanical strengthening of the Ti–Ni primary HEA

proposals.material_system: CALPHAD-designed Ti–Ni–based HEA such as Ti35Ni35V10Co10Cr10 in at%
proposals.intervention: Implement a targeted microalloying modification by introducing a controlled addition of vanadium (V) guided by CALPHAD predictions to induce a dual-phase microstructure
proposals.conditions: Prepare the alloy via arc melting followed by homogenization at 1100 °C for 4 h, then cool at controlled rates to promote formation of a fine dispersion of ordered precipitates within the BCC matrix
proposals.structural_mediator: A dual-phase microstructure consisting of a primary BCC solid solution with uniformly distributed, ordered intermetallic (Laves-type) precipitates
proposals.mechanism: Load transfer and precipitation strengthening: The dual-phase architecture improves high-temperature load bearing and impedes dislocation motion, enhancing yield strength and creep resistance
proposals.predicted_outcome: Mechanical testing at elevated temperatures (around 700 °C) will demonstrate enhanced yield strength and creep resistance (e.g., >20% improvement) relative to a single-phase Ti–Ni primary HEA without the V-induced dual-phase structure
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This strategy utilizes a compositionally guided microalloying approach, differing from both processing and coating routes, to purposefully modify phase equilibria in a Ti–Ni primary system, thereby directly targeting the improvement of high-temperature mechanical properties

decision.rationale: Direction D directly formulates a testable hypothesis by introducing a controlled aging treatment to produce a dispersion of coherent sigma precipitates in a Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy. This approach leverages well-established precipitation strengthening mechanisms to enhance elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance, with ample supporting evidence highlighting the efficacy of uniformly dispersed precipitates. Although other directions offer alternate mechanisms (e.g., microalloying with V, severe plastic deformation, or surface coatings), the controlled heat-treatment aging step in Direction D most directly targets the intrinsic strengthening of the high-entropy alloy matrix at high temperatures, making it the most straightforward and evidence-backed intervention.
